entry.title: How to build a LangGraph RAG agent with persistent memory in Redis (Beanis)

link.title: How to build a LangGraph RAG agent with persistent memory in Redis (Beanis)

entry.content:
This tutorial builds a four-node LangGraph agent: it retrieves passages from Redis by vector search, loads the session’s past turns, asks an LLM, and writes the new turns back. LangGraph runs the steps; Beanis stores the documents, embeddings and conversation history in Redis, so a restarted process picks up the same sessions.

   
Package pip install beanis (0.2.0), langgraph, langchain-openai, datasets
Code beanis · langgraph-agent example
Docs Beanis · LangGraph
Requirements Python 3.9+, Redis Stack (RediSearch for the vector index), an OpenAI API key

Setup

docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis/redis-stack:latest
pip install beanis langgraph langchain-openai datasets
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...

Step 1: models (models.py)

import time
from typing import List, Optional

from pydantic import Field
from typing_extensions import Annotated

from beanis import Document, Indexed, VectorField


class KnowledgeDocument(Document):
    title: str
    context: str
    # text-embedding-3-small returns 1536 dimensions
    embedding: Annotated[List[float], VectorField(dimensions=1536)]


class ConversationTurn(Document):
    session_id: Indexed(str)  # set index, so find(session_id=...) works
    role: str                 # "user" or "assistant"
    content: str
    ts: float = Field(default_factory=time.time)
    retrieved_docs: Optional[List[str]] = None

ts is a float on purpose: Beanis converts int and float fields back on read, which makes sorting turns simple.

Step 2: ingest 100 SQuAD passages (ingest.py)

import asyncio

from datasets import load_dataset
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
from redis.asyncio import Redis

from beanis import init_beanis
from models import KnowledgeDocument


async def main():
    redis_client = Redis(decode_responses=True)
    await init_beanis(database=redis_client, document_models=[KnowledgeDocument])

    embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small")
    rows = load_dataset("rajpurkar/squad", split="train").select(range(100))

    for row in rows:
        vector = await embeddings.aembed_query(row["context"])
        await KnowledgeDocument(
            title=row["title"], context=row["context"], embedding=vector
        ).insert()

    await redis_client.close()


asyncio.run(main())

SQuAD repeats each context for several questions, so the 100 rows contain duplicate passages. Deduplicate on context if that matters to you.

Step 3: the graph and its nodes (agent.py)

import asyncio
from typing import List, TypedDict

from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, HumanMessage, SystemMessage
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI, OpenAIEmbeddings
from langgraph.graph import END, StateGraph
from redis.asyncio import Redis

from beanis import init_beanis
from beanis.odm.indexes import IndexManager
from models import ConversationTurn, KnowledgeDocument


class AgentState(TypedDict, total=False):
    query: str
    session_id: str
    history: List[dict]
    retrieved_docs: List[str]
    context: str
    answer: str


class RAGAgent:
    def __init__(self, redis_client):
        self.redis = redis_client
        self.embeddings = OpenAIEmbeddings(model="text-embedding-3-small")
        self.llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0)
        self.graph = self._build_graph()

    def _build_graph(self):
        g = StateGraph(AgentState)
        g.add_node("retrieve", self.retrieve)
        g.add_node("load_history", self.load_history)
        g.add_node("generate", self.generate)
        g.add_node("save", self.save)
        g.set_entry_point("retrieve")
        g.add_edge("retrieve", "load_history")
        g.add_edge("load_history", "generate")
        g.add_edge("generate", "save")
        g.add_edge("save", END)
        return g.compile()

    async def retrieve(self, state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
        vector = await self.embeddings.aembed_query(state["query"])
        results = await IndexManager.find_by_vector_similarity(
            redis_client=self.redis,
            document_class=KnowledgeDocument,
            field_name="embedding",
            query_vector=vector,
            k=3,
        )
        docs = [await KnowledgeDocument.get(doc_id) for doc_id, _ in results]
        docs = [d for d in docs if d is not None]
        return {
            "retrieved_docs": [d.id for d in docs],
            "context": "\n\n".join(d.context for d in docs),
        }

    async def load_history(self, state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
        turns = await ConversationTurn.find(session_id=state["session_id"])
        turns = sorted(turns, key=lambda t: t.ts)[-6:]  # last three exchanges
        return {"history": [{"role": t.role, "content": t.content} for t in turns]}

    async def generate(self, state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
        messages = [SystemMessage(
            content="Answer from this context. If it is not there, say so.\n\n"
            + (state.get("context") or "(no context found)")
        )]
        for turn in state.get("history", []):
            cls = HumanMessage if turn["role"] == "user" else AIMessage
            messages.append(cls(content=turn["content"]))
        messages.append(HumanMessage(content=state["query"]))
        reply = await self.llm.ainvoke(messages)
        return {"answer": reply.content}

    async def save(self, state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
        await ConversationTurn(
            session_id=state["session_id"], role="user", content=state["query"]
        ).insert()
        await ConversationTurn(
            session_id=state["session_id"], role="assistant",
            content=state["answer"], retrieved_docs=state.get("retrieved_docs", []),
        ).insert()
        return state

    async def query(self, query: str, session_id: str) -> AgentState:
        return await self.graph.ainvoke({"query": query, "session_id": session_id})


async def main():
    redis_client = Redis(decode_responses=True)
    await init_beanis(
        database=redis_client,
        document_models=[KnowledgeDocument, ConversationTurn],
    )
    agent = RAGAgent(redis_client)

    for question in ["Which university is the Main Building part of?",
                     "When was it built?"]:
        result = await agent.query(question, session_id="demo")
        print(question, "->", result["answer"])

    await redis_client.close()


asyncio.run(main())

Run python ingest.py once, then python agent.py. The second question only makes sense with the first turn in history, which is what the load_history node provides. Run the script again and the history from the previous run is still in Redis.

How the memory is stored

Each turn is a Redis hash ConversationTurn:<uuid>. Its id is also added to the set idx:ConversationTurn:session_id:<session_id>, which is what find(session_id=...) reads. To drop a session:

turns = await ConversationTurn.find(session_id="demo")
await ConversationTurn.delete_many([t.id for t in turns])

delete_many deletes the hashes in one pipeline but does not touch the index set, so also run await redis_client.delete("idx:ConversationTurn:session_id:demo"). To expire old sessions automatically instead, insert turns with insert(ttl=...).

How to extend the graph

  • Branching. Use add_conditional_edges("retrieve", route_fn, {...}) to skip generation or call another tool when context is empty.
  • More retrievers. Add nodes that write to separate state keys and a merge node that combines them.
  • LangGraph checkpointing. LangGraph has its own checkpointer interface for saving graph state between steps. The history model above covers the chat turns; a checkpointer covers in-flight graph state.

Performance

The example’s README reports, for 100 documents on an M1 Mac, 10 to 20 ms for the Redis vector search and 500 to 800 ms per full query. Most of the time is the LLM call.

Questions people ask

Does LangGraph need Redis to keep memory? No. LangGraph has its own checkpointers. This post stores chat turns as Beanis documents so they are plain Redis hashes you can query, expire and inspect.

Why is my conversation history empty? session_id must be declared Indexed(str); find() only queries indexed fields and raises ValueError otherwise. Also check that the same session_id is passed on every call.

Can I use a local embedding model instead of OpenAI? Yes. Change VectorField(dimensions=...) to the model’s output size, re-ingest, and embed queries with the same model.

Do I need Redis Stack or is plain Redis enough? The vector index uses RediSearch, so this agent needs Redis Stack. Conversation history alone would work on plain Redis.

Links

  • PyPI: pypi.org/project/beanis
  • GitHub: github.com/andreim14/beanis
  • Docs: andreim14.github.io/beanis
  • Example: beanis-examples/langgraph-agent
  • Related: RAG retrieval with Beanis · Geo search with Beanis
entry.summary: A LangGraph agent that retrieves passages with Beanis vector search, keeps conversation history in Redis, and answers with an OpenAI model. Models, graph, nodes and entry point in complete Python.

entry.title: LLM-Oasis: a large-scale dataset and benchmark for end-to-end factuality evaluation of LLM text (Computational Linguistics 2026)

link.title: LLM-Oasis: a large-scale dataset and benchmark for end-to-end factuality evaluation of LLM text (Computational Linguistics 2026)

entry.content:
LLM-Oasis is a resource for training and testing systems that decide whether a whole piece of text is factual, not just a single isolated claim. It is built from Wikipedia: each passage gets a paraphrased factual version and an unfactual version that differs by one subtle falsified claim, giving 81k ⟨factual, unfactual⟩ pairs for training and a human-validated gold benchmark for testing. The task is hard: GPT-4o reaches 60.8% balanced accuracy zero-shot and 68.0% with retrieved Wikipedia evidence, where 50% is chance.

   
Paper Truth or Mirage? Towards End-to-End Factuality Evaluation with LLM-Oasis, Computational Linguistics 52(1):1–41, 2026 · arXiv 2411.19655
Authors Alessandro Scirè*, Andrei Stefan Bejgu*, Simone Tedeschi, Karim Ghonim, Federico Martelli, Roberto Navigli (* equal contribution). Babelscape and Sapienza University of Rome
Data Hugging Face collection: 4 training datasets (one per pipeline step) and the gold claim verification set, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
Code github.com/Babelscape/LLM-Oasis
Use it for Training claim extractors, retrievers and claim verifiers; benchmarking LLMs as end-to-end factuality evaluators or as evidence-based claim verifiers

Use it

The public datasets are on the Hugging Face Hub under Babelscape/. Column names and split sizes below come from the Hub’s dataset viewer API.

Dataset Columns Splits
LLM-Oasis_claim_extraction title, text, claims train 67,426 · validation 13,849
LLM-Oasis_claim_falsification title, text, factual_claim, unfactual_claim train 42,749 · validation 9,641
LLM-Oasis_paraphrase_generation title, text, claims, paraphrase train 67,419 · validation 13,848
LLM-Oasis_unfactual_text_generation title, text, unfactual_claims, paraphrase, unfactual_text train 67,385 · validation 13,838
LLM-Oasis_claim_verification (gold, Task 2) id, claim, evidence gold 2,656

Train plus validation adds up to about 81K rows per step, in line with the 81,275 pages in the paper. The falsification release is smaller (52,390 rows) than the 81,275 falsified claims reported in Table 2.

The unfactual text dataset already holds both sides of each pair: paraphrase is the factual text and unfactual_text is the version with the falsified claim. That is enough to build a binary training set for an end-to-end factuality classifier:

from datasets import load_dataset

pairs = load_dataset("Babelscape/LLM-Oasis_unfactual_text_generation", split="train")

def to_examples(batch):
    texts = batch["paraphrase"] + batch["unfactual_text"]
    labels = [True] * len(batch["paraphrase"]) + [False] * len(batch["unfactual_text"])
    return {"text": texts, "factual": labels}

train = pairs.map(to_examples, batched=True, remove_columns=pairs.column_names)

# Task 2 gold set: one claim and one evidence passage per row, labels withheld
gold = load_dataset("Babelscape/LLM-Oasis_claim_verification", split="gold")

The gold data for both tasks is released without labels for blind evaluation. For Task 1 the README links a submission form: you upload a .jsonl file with one {"id": ..., "factual": true/false} entry per text, where id matches Babelscape/LLM-Oasis_e2e_factuality_evaluation. At the time of writing, the Hub API reports that dataset as not accessible without authentication.

How it was built

The source is English Wikipedia, restricted to the most visited pages. Each page is split into passages of K = 5 sentences with a sliding window of stride 1, and one passage per page is sampled. GPT-4 then runs four steps on each passage in a single unified prompt (Table 1 of the paper):

The paper’s running example shows the style of error. From a passage on the Amazon rainforest, the claim “Brazil contains 60% of the rainforest” becomes “The majority of the forest is contained within Peru”: another country the rainforest covers, so the error is plausible in context.

The result (Table 2): 81,275 pages, 681,201 claims (8.4 per passage on average), 81,275 falsified claims, and 81,275 factual plus 81,275 unfactual texts of about 83 and 87 tokens.

Human validation. Five expert linguists checked 1,750 instances per step, with 100 shared by all annotators to measure agreement (Table 3):

Step Accuracy Fleiss’ κ
Claim extraction 96.78% 0.81
Claim falsification 98.55% 0.84
Factual text generation 90.36% 0.73
Unfactual text generation 89.20% 0.72

Gold benchmark. Only instances that no annotator flagged as an error at any stage are kept; texts flagged for omitting a detail are discarded too. From these the paper defines two tasks:

  • Task 1, end-to-end factuality evaluation: given a text, output True if it is factual and False if it contains an inaccuracy. Inputs are only the generated factual and unfactual texts, never the original Wikipedia passage. About 2k instances.
  • Task 2, evidence-based claim verification: given one claim and one evidence passage (the factual text), output whether the evidence supports the claim. Original claims are labelled True, their falsified versions False.

A baseline built from the training data. The paper also trains a small modular system on the silver data: a T5-base claim extractor, an E5-base dense retriever trained on about 3.2M ⟨claim, evidence⟩ pairs, and a DeBERTa-v3-large NLI claim verifier trained on 3.2M triplets. A text counts as factual only if every extracted claim is verified against the retrieved passages. Fine-tuning lifts the retriever’s Recall@30 from 0.52 to 0.95.

Results

The metric is balanced accuracy (%) on the gold benchmark, so a random guess scores 50. Open-weight models are averaged over five seeds. “E2E” is Task 1, “claim verif.” is Task 2.

Model Size E2E zero-shot E2E with retrieval Claim verif. zero-shot Claim verif. best prompt
Fine-tuned pipeline (ours) 1B / 0.4B n/a 69.24 n/a 93.30
GPT-4o n/a 60.8 68.0 89.49 93.93
Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct 70B 59.2 58.8 91.79 94.08
Phi-4 14B 57.2 57.6 84.14 92.69
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 7B 55.8 54.7 84.85 87.11
Falcon3-Mamba-7B-Instruct 7B 55.3 51.0 63.45 74.98
Phi-4-mini-instruct 4B 54.4 56.3 70.50 84.06
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 8B 53.6 54.1 78.56 86.55
Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 7B 51.2 50.5 72.87 80.67

Sources: Tables 5, 6 and 7. The fine-tuned row is the full 1B pipeline on Task 1 and the 0.4B claim verifier alone on Task 2. “Best prompt” is the highest of zero-shot, few-shot and their explain-then-answer variants.

What the numbers say:

  • End-to-end factuality evaluation is hard. Open-weight LLMs score between 51.2 and 59.2 zero-shot. The best open-weight score in any prompt setting is 61.7 (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, few-shot, Table 4).
  • Retrieval mostly does not help LLMs. With the top 30 retrieved passages, most models stay flat or drop. GPT-4o is the exception, going from 60.8 to 68.0. Truncating the RAG prompt from 18k down to 2k tokens leaves performance roughly stable (Figure 3), so long context alone is not the cause.
  • A small specialised pipeline wins. The 1B pipeline trained on LLM-Oasis reaches 69.24, above every LLM tested, including GPT-4o with retrieval.
  • Claim verification is much easier than end-to-end evaluation. With the right evidence given and a single claim of about 100 tokens of context (against about 4k in the end-to-end task), best-prompt scores rise to between 74.98 and 94.08. The 0.4B verifier reaches 93.30, close to Llama-3.3-70B (94.08) and GPT-4o (93.93) in their best settings.

Limitations

  • The training data is LLM-generated. Human checks show 89 to 99% accuracy per step, but errors remain. The authors recommend the silver data for building systems and the gold benchmark for evaluation.
  • One prompt for all four steps. Generation used a single GPT-4 call per passage instead of multi-step prompting, mainly to save cost (multi-step would have cost about four times as much). A qualitative comparison showed no clear quality gain from multi-step.
  • Wikipedia changes. Unfactual texts stay unfactual, but factual texts can become outdated as pages are revised.
  • Popular pages only. Long-tail facts are not targeted, though popular pages still contain lesser-known details.
  • English only. Other languages and domains are left to future work.
  • Non-commercial license. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

Questions people ask

How is LLM-Oasis different from FEVER? FEVER has 185,445 human-written claims built from about 10k Wikipedia pages and asks you to verify one claim at a time. LLM-Oasis asks whether a multi-sentence text is factual, with the error hidden in one of several claims, and covers 81,275 pages. The falsification prompt rules out simple negations and changes to dates, numbers or names, aiming for plausible substitutions rather than flipped verbs.

How is it different from FACTOR or FELM? Both are benchmarks: FACTOR has 4,266 instances and FELM 847 LLM outputs. LLM-Oasis is large enough to train factuality evaluators, with 81k text pairs and 681,201 claims, and it is not tied to one task such as summarisation.

What tasks does it support? Two benchmark tasks: end-to-end factuality evaluation of raw text (Task 1) and evidence-based claim verification (Task 2). The four training datasets also cover claim extraction, claim falsification and factual or unfactual text generation as separate supervised tasks.

How do I evaluate my LLM on it? For Task 1, predict True or False for each text in Babelscape/LLM-Oasis_e2e_factuality_evaluation (not publicly accessible on the Hub at the time of writing) and submit the .jsonl through the form in the README; results are reported as balanced accuracy. For Task 2, the gold claim-evidence pairs are public in Babelscape/LLM-Oasis_claim_verification, also without labels; the README does not describe a separate submission route.

Can I train on it? Yes. The four silver datasets have train and validation splits, and the paper’s baseline fine-tunes T5, E5 and DeBERTa models on them. Use is limited to non-commercial purposes under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

Does giving the model Wikipedia evidence solve the task? Not for most LLMs. At 18k tokens the passage needed to verify a text is in the retrieved evidence 95% of the time, yet most open-weight models score about the same as without it. The difficulty is using the evidence, not finding it.

Cite

@article{10.1162/COLI.a.575,
    author = {Scirè, Alessandro and Bejgu, Andrei Stefan and Tedeschi, Simone and Ghonim, Karim and Martelli, Federico and Navigli, Roberto},
    title = {Truth or Mirage? Towards End-To-End Factuality Evaluation with LLM-Oasis},
    journal = {Computational Linguistics},
    volume = {52},
    number = {1},
    pages = {1-41},
    year = {2026},
    issn = {0891-2017},
    doi = {10.1162/COLI.a.575},
    url = {https://doi.org/10.1162/COLI.a.575}
}

Paper: MIT Press · arXiv · Code: GitHub · Data: Hugging Face collection
entry.summary: LLM-Oasis is built from 81,275 Wikipedia pages: 681,201 extracted claims and 81k pairs of factual and unfactual texts that differ by one subtle falsified claim. On its human-validated gold benchmark GPT-4o reaches 60.8% balanced accuracy zero-shot and 68.0% with retrieval; a 1B fine-tuned pipeline reaches 69.24%.

entry.title: Concept-pedia and Concept-10k: test your vision-language model beyond ImageNet (EMNLP 2025)

link.title: Concept-pedia and Concept-10k: test your vision-language model beyond ImageNet (EMNLP 2025)

entry.content:
Concept-10k is a benchmark for one question: does your vision-language model recognise concepts outside ImageNet? It has 9,837 concepts across 28 semantic categories, each checked by two expert linguists. Models that look excellent on ImageNet do not hold up on it: SigLIP-SO400M goes from 83.2% top-1 on ImageNet-1k to 40.3% on Concept-10k.

It comes from Concept-pedia, a training set of 165K concepts built automatically from Wikipedia image captions and the BabelNet taxonomy. Fine-tuning on it adds 5.2 points on Concept-10k on average, without losing ImageNet-1k accuracy.

   
Paper Concept-pedia: a Wide-coverage Semantically-annotated Multimodal Dataset, EMNLP 2025
Authors Karim Ghonim, Andrei Stefan Bejgu, Alberte Fernández-Castro, Roberto Navigli (Sapienza University of Rome, Babelscape)
Benchmark sapienzanlp/Concept-10k on Hugging Face, one test split
Fine-tuned models sapienzanlp SigLIP base, large and SO400M, fine-tuned on Concept-pedia
Use it for zero-shot image classification evals, long-tail and abstract concepts, per-category error analysis

Evaluate your model on Concept-10k

Each row is one image with the concept it shows, its BabelNet id and its semantic category:

{"id": "147_000015482", "caption": "Bipartite patella", "concept": "patella",
 "bn_id": "bn:00049315n", "category": "PART", "image": <PIL.Image>}

Zero-shot evaluation works like the paper’s: embed every concept name and every image in the same space, predict the concept with the highest similarity, report top-1 accuracy. This script does that for any SigLIP or CLIP checkpoint on Hugging Face:

# pip install torch transformers datasets   (tested with transformers 5.22)
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor

model_id = "google/siglip-base-patch16-224"   # or any CLIP / SigLIP checkpoint
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_id).to(device).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)

ds = load_dataset("sapienzanlp/Concept-10k", split="test")
concepts = sorted(set(ds["concept"]))
names = [c.replace("_", " ") for c in concepts]      # "dangerous_goods" -> "dangerous goods"
index = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(concepts)}

def unit(x):
    # transformers >= 5 returns an output object, older versions a tensor
    x = x if torch.is_tensor(x) else x.pooler_output
    return torch.nn.functional.normalize(x, dim=-1)

with torch.no_grad():
    text = []
    for i in range(0, len(names), 512):
        t = processor(text=names[i:i + 512], padding="max_length", truncation=True, return_tensors="pt").to(device)
        text.append(unit(model.get_text_features(**t)))
    text = torch.cat(text)

    correct = 0
    for i in range(0, len(ds), 64):
        batch = ds[i:i + 64]
        px = processor(images=[im.convert("RGB") for im in batch["image"]], return_tensors="pt").to(device)
        img = unit(model.get_image_features(**px))
        pred = (img @ text.T).argmax(dim=-1).tolist()
        correct += sum(p == index[c] for p, c in zip(pred, batch["concept"]))

print(f"Concept-10k top-1: {correct / len(ds):.1%}")

The label space is every concept in the benchmark (about 9.8K candidates), which is what makes it hard. To compare against the paper’s numbers, use the same models; the public release has 34,345 rows, so small differences from the paper’s tables are expected. Group the predictions by category to see where a model breaks, which is usually more useful than the single number.

To classify your own images, the fine-tuned checkpoints drop into the standard zero-shot pipeline:

from transformers import pipeline

clf = pipeline("zero-shot-image-classification",
               model="sapienzanlp/siglip-base-patch16-256-ft-concept-pedia")
clf("photo.jpg", candidate_labels=["moka pot", "french press", "espresso machine"])

Results

The full numbers, including ImageNet-v2. “Fine-tuned” means trained on Concept-pedia with all Concept-10k images removed first.

Model Params ImageNet-1k ImageNet-v2 Concept-10k
CLIP-B 150M 68.3 61.9 22.0
CLIP-L 428M 75.5 69.0 26.7
SigLIP-B 203M 76.2 69.6 31.1
SigLIP-B, fine-tuned 203M 75.9 69.1 36.1
SigLIP-L 652M 80.5 74.2 36.1
SigLIP-L, fine-tuned 652M 79.3 73.5 41.9
SigLIP-SO400M 878M 83.2 77.2 40.3
SigLIP-SO400M, fine-tuned 878M 83.0 76.7 45.0

Three things to take from it:

  • The drop is about which concepts you test, not image quality. On Concept-1k, the slice of Concept-pedia restricted to ImageNet’s 1,000 classes, human annotators judged labels correct 95.7% of the time against 88.4% for ImageNet itself. Models still score lower there (SigLIP-large: 87.6% on ImageNet vs 83.0% on Concept-1k), the same pattern as ImageNet-v2. New concepts, not bad data, cause the gap.
  • Abstract and specialised categories are the weak spot. Even after fine-tuning, SigLIP-SO400M sits at 23.1% on law, 24.1% on psychology and 26.0% on measures, against 71.9% on animals (Table 7).
  • Fine-tuning helps everywhere it matters and costs nothing on ImageNet. +5.2 points on Concept-10k on average; ImageNet-1k accuracy moves by at most 1.2 points.

How the data was built

The idea: Wikipedia editors have already linked millions of images to concepts by hand. Concept-pedia reuses those links instead of paying for new labels.

A caption often mentions a concept without linking it, while the page body links the same term. Link propagation copies that link onto the caption.
  1. Start from captions. 4.6 million image captions from English Wikipedia (Nov 2023 dump).
  2. Link propagation. When a caption mentions something the page body already links, copy the link onto the caption. Four matching rules, each measured on 200 samples: exact string (100% precision), lemma (91%), BabelNet synonym such as natatorium → swimming pool (96%), and Wikipedia redirect such as Lesser Panda → Red Panda (84%). Afterwards 74.5% of captions carry at least one link. Every annotation records which rule produced it, so you can keep only the high-precision ones.
  3. Taxonomic propagation. About 85% of the links point to named entities, not concepts. Each entity is mapped to its concept through BabelNet’s hypernyms (Arrie Church → church), and rare concepts move up to their parent (Hokuto → train) until every concept has at least 5 images. Precision of this step: 96%. Result: 101,354 concepts, each with 5+ images.
  4. Concept-10k. From concepts with at least 10 images: drop captions that mention more than one concept, keep the 5 shortest captions per concept, and remove concepts that are parents of other concepts in the set (keep race car, drop car) so a correct prediction is never marked wrong. Two expert linguists then validated every image-concept pair (Cohen’s κ = 89.3). Final benchmark: 49,185 image-concept pairs over 9,837 concepts.
ImageNet-1k covers 11 of the 29 semantic categories; Concept-10k covers 28, including abstract ones such as events and feelings, with a more even spread.

Concepts are labelled with the 29 semantic categories of CNER (Martinelli et al., 2024). That is where the category column comes from, and it is what makes per-category error analysis possible.

Limitations

  • Captions come only from English Wikipedia, which brings a cultural bias.
  • The benchmark keeps one concept per image; real images often show several.
  • Concepts were chosen by frequency, so diversity inside a category is not optimised.

Questions people ask

Is Concept-10k a replacement for ImageNet? No, a complement. ImageNet tells you how well a model fits a well-studied set of 1,000 classes; Concept-10k tells you whether it generalises to the long tail.

Why are the numbers so low? The label space is ~9.8K concepts, many abstract or specialised, and a prediction is right only if it names exactly the annotated concept. Parents of other concepts were removed, so a more general answer does not count as wrong by accident.

Can I train on Concept-10k? No, it is a test set. Train on Concept-pedia (with the Concept-10k images removed, as in the paper) or on your own data, then evaluate here.

Which fine-tuned model should I use? siglip-base-patch16-256-ft-concept-pedia for speed, siglip-so400m-patch14-384-ft-concept-pedia for accuracy, siglip-large-patch16-256-ft-concept-pedia in between.

Cite

If you use Concept-pedia, Concept-10k or the fine-tuned models, please cite:

@inproceedings{ghonim-etal-2025-concept,
    title = "Concept-pedia: a Wide-coverage Semantically-annotated Multimodal Dataset",
    author = "Ghonim, Karim and Bejgu, Andrei Stefan and Fern{\'a}ndez-Castro, Alberte and Navigli, Roberto",
    booktitle = "Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing",
    month = nov,
    year = "2025",
    address = "Suzhou, China",
    publisher = "Association for Computational Linguistics",
    url = "https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1745/",
    doi = "10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.1745",
    pages = "34417--34438"
}

Paper: ACL Anthology · PDF · Benchmark: Concept-10k · Models: sapienzanlp
entry.summary: Concept-10k is a human-validated benchmark of 9,837 visual concepts in 28 semantic categories. SigLIP-SO400M scores 83.2% on ImageNet-1k and 40.3% on Concept-10k. How the dataset was built from Wikipedia and BabelNet, how to evaluate your own model on it in a few lines, and how to cite it.

entry.title: How to find nearby places in Redis with Python: a restaurant finder with Beanis GeoPoint

link.title: How to find nearby places in Redis with Python: a restaurant finder with Beanis GeoPoint

entry.content:
This tutorial stores restaurants in Redis with a geo-indexed GeoPoint field and answers “what is within 2 km of me?” with one call. It then shows how the restaurant-finder example uses that index as a cache in front of PostgreSQL/PostGIS.

   
Package pip install beanis (0.2.0)
Code beanis · restaurant-finder example
Docs Geo-spatial guide · andreim14.github.io/beanis
Requirements Python 3.9+, Redis 5+ (no modules; geo commands are built in)

Minimal example

docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7
pip install beanis

import asyncio

from redis.asyncio import Redis
from typing_extensions import Annotated

from beanis import Document, GeoPoint, Indexed, init_beanis
from beanis.odm.indexes import IndexedField, IndexManager


class Restaurant(Document):
    name: str
    cuisine: Indexed(str)
    rating: Indexed(float)
    location: Annotated[GeoPoint, IndexedField()]  # GEOADD on insert


async def main():
    redis_client = Redis(decode_responses=True)
    await init_beanis(database=redis_client, document_models=[Restaurant])

    for r in [
        Restaurant(name="Near the Colosseum", cuisine="italian", rating=4.6,
                   location=GeoPoint(longitude=12.4930, latitude=41.8925)),
        Restaurant(name="Trastevere", cuisine="italian", rating=4.2,
                   location=GeoPoint(longitude=12.4700, latitude=41.8890)),
        Restaurant(name="Termini", cuisine="japanese", rating=4.4,
                   location=GeoPoint(longitude=12.5010, latitude=41.9010)),
    ]:
        await r.insert()

    hits = await IndexManager.find_by_geo_radius_with_distance(
        redis_client=redis_client,
        document_class=Restaurant,
        field_name="location",
        longitude=12.4922,   # Colosseum
        latitude=41.8902,
        radius=2,
        unit="km",
    )
    hits.sort(key=lambda h: h[1])  # results are not sorted by distance

    for doc_id, distance in hits:
        r = await Restaurant.get(doc_id)
        print(f"{distance:.2f} km  {r.name} ({r.cuisine}, {r.rating})")

    await redis_client.close()


asyncio.run(main())

GeoPoint takes longitude and latitude as keyword arguments and rejects values outside -180..180 and -90..90.

Insert with insert(), not insert_many(). In Beanis 0.2.0 insert_many() writes the hashes in one pipeline but does not update the geo or field indexes, so the documents would not show up in radius queries.

How the geo index works

On insert, Beanis writes the hash Restaurant:<id> and runs GEOADD idx:Restaurant:location <lon> <lat> <id>. A radius query is a GEORADIUS on that key. Redis stores geo members in a sorted set scored by geohash, so the lookup does not compute distances against every row.

Two functions are available:

Function Returns
IndexManager.find_by_geo_radius(...) list of ids
IndexManager.find_by_geo_radius_with_distance(...) list of (id, distance) in the requested unit

Both take redis_client, document_class, field_name, longitude, latitude, radius and unit ("m", "km", "mi", "ft"; default "km"). Neither sorts by distance, so sort in Python when order matters.

How to filter nearby results by cuisine or rating

A geo query returns ids. Combine it with the other indexes using set intersection:

nearby = dict(await IndexManager.find_by_geo_radius_with_distance(
    redis_client, Restaurant, "location", 12.4922, 41.8902, 2, unit="km"
))
good_italian = {r.id for r in await Restaurant.find(cuisine="italian", rating__gte=4.5)}

ids = sorted(nearby.keys() & good_italian, key=nearby.get)
restaurants = await Restaurant.get_many(ids)

The restaurant-finder example does the simpler version: it loads every document in the radius and filters on the fields in Python.

How to use Redis as a geo cache in front of PostgreSQL

In the example, PostgreSQL with PostGIS is the source of truth (OpenStreetMap data is imported there), and Redis holds a RestaurantCache copy with the geo index:

A sketch of that flow, with your own PostgreSQL loader passed in:

async def nearby(redis_client, lon, lat, radius_km, load_from_postgres):
    hits = await IndexManager.find_by_geo_radius_with_distance(
        redis_client, Restaurant, "location", lon, lat, radius_km, unit="km"
    )
    if hits:
        hits.sort(key=lambda h: h[1])
        docs = await Restaurant.get_many([doc_id for doc_id, _ in hits])
        live = [d for d in docs if d is not None]  # None: hash expired or deleted
        if live:
            return live

    rows = await load_from_postgres(lon, lat, radius_km)  # your PostGIS query
    docs = [
        Restaurant(
            id=str(row["id"]),
            name=row["name"],
            cuisine=row["cuisine"],
            rating=row["rating"],
            location=GeoPoint(longitude=row["lon"], latitude=row["lat"]),
        )
        for row in rows
    ]
    for doc in docs:
        await doc.insert()  # insert() also updates the geo and field indexes
    return docs

Using the PostgreSQL id as the Redis id means a later change can target the same key.

How to keep the cache fresh

  • Expire entries. await doc.insert(ttl=3600) or default_ttl in class Settings. The hash expires, but its id stays in the index sets, so get() returns None for it. The sketch above skips those and goes to PostgreSQL when nothing live is left.
  • Invalidate on write. When a restaurant changes in PostgreSQL, call await Restaurant.delete(str(db_id)). It deletes the hash and removes the id from the geo and field indexes. The next miss reloads it.
  • Replace on write. Delete, then insert the new version. Prefer this over update() for indexed fields like location, cuisine or rating, since update() writes the hash fields only.

Performance

The geo guide reports about 0.2 ms per radius query. The repo also has a geo benchmark you can run on your own hardware: benchmarks/benchmark_geospatial.py. End-to-end API time is a different number: the restaurant-finder README reports first and cached calls of the same order (about 650 ms and 620 ms on 2,643 Paris restaurants), so profile the document loading and filtering around the geo lookup before expecting large gains from the cache.

Run the full example

git clone https://github.com/andreim14/beanis-examples.git
cd beanis-examples/restaurant-finder
pip install -r requirements.txt

docker run -d --name restaurant-postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_USER=restaurant_user \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=restaurant_pass \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=restaurant_db \
  -p 5432:5432 postgis/postgis:15-3.3
docker run -d --name restaurant-redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine

python main.py   # FastAPI on :8000, leave it running
# in a second terminal: import Rome from OpenStreetMap, then run the demo
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/import/area?lat=41.8902&lon=12.4922&radius_km=5"
python demo.py

Questions people ask

Does Redis geo search need Redis Stack? No. GEOADD and GEORADIUS are core Redis commands, and Beanis’s geo index uses only those.

Are the results sorted by distance? Not in Beanis 0.2.0. Both radius functions call GEORADIUS without a sort option, so sort the (id, distance) list yourself.

Can I query by bounding box or polygon? Beanis exposes radius queries only. For polygons keep using PostGIS.

Why use Redis if PostGIS already does radius queries? To move repeated read traffic off the primary database. PostGIS stays the source of truth and Redis holds a disposable copy you can rebuild from it.

What happens if Redis loses the data? Nothing permanent. Every request becomes a miss until the cache is warm again from PostgreSQL.

Links

  • PyPI: pypi.org/project/beanis
  • GitHub: github.com/andreim14/beanis
  • Docs: andreim14.github.io/beanis
  • Example: beanis-examples/restaurant-finder
  • Redis geospatial commands: redis.io
entry.summary: Store restaurants with a GeoPoint in Redis using Beanis, query them by radius with GEORADIUS, and use Redis as a geo cache in front of PostgreSQL/PostGIS. Complete async Python code.

entry.title: Word Sense Linking: disambiguate word senses in raw text, no pre-marked spans (Findings of ACL 2024)

link.title: Word Sense Linking: disambiguate word senses in raw text, no pre-marked spans (Findings of ACL 2024)

entry.content:
Word Sense Linking (WSL) is word sense disambiguation that works on plain text. Classic WSD needs someone to mark which words to disambiguate and to list each word’s possible senses first. WSL takes the raw sentence and a sense inventory (WordNet) and does all three steps itself: it finds the spans, retrieves the candidate senses, and picks the right one, in a single forward pass.

   
Paper Word Sense Linking: Disambiguating Outside the Sandbox, Findings of ACL 2024
Authors Andrei Stefan Bejgu, Edoardo Barba, Luigi Procopio, Alberte Fernández-Castro, Roberto Navigli (Babelscape, Sapienza University of Rome)
Model Babelscape/wsl-base · all resources in the Hugging Face collection
Code github.com/Babelscape/WSL
Headline result 75.9 F1 on raw text, against 71.5 for ConSeC, the strongest WSD system adapted to the same setting

Run it

git clone https://github.com/Babelscape/WSL
cd WSL
pip install .
# if import fails with "No module named pkg_resources": pip install "setuptools<70"

from wsl import WSL

model = WSL.from_pretrained("Babelscape/wsl-base")
model("Bus drivers drive busses for a living.")

WSLOutput(
    text='Bus drivers drive busses for a living.',
    spans=[
        Span(start=0,  end=11, label='bus driver: someone who drives a bus', text='Bus drivers'),
        Span(start=12, end=17, label='drive: operate or control a vehicle', text='drive'),
        Span(start=18, end=24, label='bus: a vehicle carrying many passengers; used for public transport', text='busses'),
        Span(start=31, end=37, label='living: the financial means whereby one lives', text='living'),
    ],
)

You pass a sentence; you get back character offsets, the matched text and a WordNet gloss for every span the model decided to disambiguate. Note that it found the multiword bus driver on its own and that living got the “means of support” sense, not the “being alive” one.

Why WSD needed a new task

State-of-the-art WSD systems score above the estimated inter-annotator agreement on the standard benchmarks, yet almost nobody uses them in real pipelines. The paper’s argument is that the standard setup quietly assumes three things are given:

  1. A sense inventory (for example WordNet). Unavoidable, and fine.
  2. The spans to disambiguate. Someone already decided that bank and cover are the words that matter. On raw text, nobody did.
  3. The candidate senses for each span, from a hand-built word-to-sense mapping. Such mappings are incomplete for most languages other than English.

WSL keeps (1) and drops (2) and (3). That is the setting of real applications such as machine translation, information extraction or retrieval: you have text and an inventory, nothing else.

How it works

Pipelines that first find spans and then look up their senses have a chicken-and-egg problem: to know whether bus drivers is one span you need to know a sense bus driver exists. WSL flips the order.

  • Retriever. Each sense is turned into text (its lemmas plus its definition) and embedded once. The input window is embedded and the 100 closest senses become the candidates. It is trained with a contrastive objective using hard negatives, so similar-but-wrong senses get pushed away.
  • Reader. The window and its 100 candidate senses are concatenated into one sequence. Start and end heads mark the spans; a third head matches each span to a candidate. Because the text tokens attend to the candidate senses, span detection is informed by what senses exist.
  • Speed. Everything after retrieval is one encoder pass per window. On the standard WSD test set (7,253 instances) it runs in under 17 seconds, against 73 seconds for ConSeC on the same GPU.

The benchmark and the results

You cannot measure precision on raw text if the gold data only annotates some of the words: a correct prediction on an unannotated word would count as a false positive. So the paper also releases a fully annotated version of the standard WSD evaluation set, taking it from 7,253 to 11,623 annotations so every content word is covered (inter-annotator agreement κ = 0.83).

Setting System Precision Recall F1
Spans and candidates given (classic WSD, ALL) ConSeC     82.0
  WSL     80.2
Raw text, spans not given BEM + heuristic spans 76.6 61.2 68.0
  ConSeC + heuristic spans 80.4 64.3 71.5
  WSL 75.2 76.7 75.9
  • The gain is recall. WSL finds 92.1% of the gold spans; the best alternative span detector finds 80.6%. ConSeC is more precise on the spans it gets, but misses many more.
  • Classic WSD is not the bottleneck. In the classic setting WSL is within 2 points of ConSeC while being about 4 times faster. Its advantage appears exactly when the sandbox assumptions are removed.
  • Training data matters. SemCor, the standard training corpus, leaves many words unannotated. The paper fills them in (133,727 new annotations on top of 226,036), which helps WSL learn when not to skip a word.

When to use it

  • Lexical features for search or RAG: disambiguate query and document terms to WordNet senses before matching.
  • Information extraction and knowledge bases: link content words to a sense inventory, not just named entities to Wikipedia.
  • Lower-resource settings: the retriever does not depend on a word-to-sense mapping, so you can plug in an inventory with definitions but poor lemma coverage.
  • Linguistic analysis at scale: sense-tagged corpora without manual pre-annotation.

The released model is English, trained on SemCor with WordNet senses. Other languages need a sense inventory with definitions and training data in that language.

Questions people ask

How is WSL different from WSD? WSD picks a sense for spans someone already chose, from candidates someone already listed. WSL starts from the raw text and does span detection, candidate generation and disambiguation itself.

How is it different from entity linking? Entity linking connects names (Paris, Barack Obama) to an encyclopedia. WSL connects common words and multiword expressions (bus driver, drive, living) to the senses of a dictionary like WordNet. The architecture borrows the retriever-reader design from entity linking.

Which sense inventory does it use? WordNet (English). The retriever only needs a textual definition for each sense, so other inventories can be plugged in by re-indexing.

Is the fully annotated evaluation set available? Yes: Babelscape/wsl on Hugging Face (dev and test splits). The retriever, reader and WordNet index are also released as separate models in the same collection.

Cite

@inproceedings{bejgu-etal-2024-word,
    title = "Word Sense Linking: Disambiguating Outside the Sandbox",
    author = "Bejgu, Andrei Stefan and Barba, Edoardo and Procopio, Luigi and Fern{\'a}ndez-Castro, Alberte and Navigli, Roberto",
    booktitle = "Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024",
    month = aug,
    year = "2024",
    address = "Bangkok, Thailand",
    publisher = "Association for Computational Linguistics",
    url = "https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.851/",
    doi = "10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.851",
    pages = "14332--14347"
}

Paper: ACL Anthology · PDF · Code: Babelscape/WSL · Model: Babelscape/wsl-base
entry.summary: Word Sense Linking (WSL) finds which words in a raw text need disambiguating and links each to its WordNet sense, in one forward pass. 75.9 F1 on the fully annotated benchmark against 71.5 for the best WSD system adapted to the task. How it works, how to run it, and how to cite it.

entry.title: How to build RAG retrieval on Redis with Beanis vector search

link.title: How to build RAG retrieval on Redis with Beanis vector search

entry.content:
This tutorial builds the retrieval half of a RAG pipeline on Redis: a Beanis model with a VectorField, an ingest step that stores text plus embeddings, and a search function that returns the closest passages. At the end you have one Python file that you can point at your own documents and plug into any LLM prompt.

   
Package pip install beanis (0.2.0)
Code beanis · simple-rag example
Docs andreim14.github.io/beanis
Requirements Python 3.9+, Redis Stack (needs the RediSearch module for vector indexes), transformers>=4.52 and torch>=2.6 for the embedding model

Minimal example

Start Redis Stack:

docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis/redis-stack:latest
pip install beanis "transformers>=4.52" "torch>=2.6" peft torchvision pillow

Then save this as rag.py and run python rag.py:

import asyncio
from typing import List

from redis.asyncio import Redis
from transformers import AutoModel
from typing_extensions import Annotated

from beanis import Document, VectorField, init_beanis
from beanis.odm.indexes import IndexManager

DIM = 1024

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("jinaai/jina-embeddings-v4", trust_remote_code=True)


def embed(text: str, kind: str) -> List[float]:
    """kind is "passage" when indexing and "query" when searching."""
    vec = model.encode_text(
        texts=[text], task="retrieval", prompt_name=kind, truncate_dim=DIM
    )[0]
    return vec.tolist()


class KnowledgeBase(Document):
    text: str
    embedding: Annotated[List[float], VectorField(dimensions=DIM)]


async def search(redis_client, query: str, k: int = 3):
    results = await IndexManager.find_by_vector_similarity(
        redis_client=redis_client,
        document_class=KnowledgeBase,
        field_name="embedding",
        query_vector=embed(query, "query"),
        k=k,
    )
    hits = []
    for doc_id, score in results:
        doc = await KnowledgeBase.get(doc_id)
        if doc is not None:
            hits.append((score, doc.text))
    return hits


async def main():
    redis_client = Redis(decode_responses=True)
    # Creates the HNSW index idx:KnowledgeBase:vector if it does not exist
    await init_beanis(database=redis_client, document_models=[KnowledgeBase])

    for text in [
        "Redis keeps its whole dataset in memory.",
        "Beanis maps Pydantic models to Redis hashes.",
        "HNSW is a graph index for approximate nearest neighbour search.",
    ]:
        await KnowledgeBase(text=text, embedding=embed(text, "passage")).insert()

    for score, text in await search(redis_client, "How does approximate vector search work?"):
        print(f"{score:.3f}  {text}")

    await redis_client.close()


asyncio.run(main())

The score is the distance RediSearch returns for the KNN query. With the default COSINE metric, lower means closer.

How to define a vector field

embedding: Annotated[List[float], VectorField(dimensions=1024)]

VectorField takes these parameters, all with defaults except dimensions:

Parameter Default Meaning
dimensions required must equal the length of your embeddings
algorithm "HNSW" or "FLAT" for exact search on small sets
distance_metric "COSINE" or "L2", "IP"
m 16 HNSW links per node
ef_construction 200 HNSW build-time candidate list size

At init_beanis() Beanis runs FT.CREATE idx:<ClassName>:vector over hashes with the <ClassName>: prefix, using a FLOAT32 vector field. If RediSearch is not available it prints a warning and continues, so check the output if search returns nothing.

How to search and tune recall

results = await IndexManager.find_by_vector_similarity(
    redis_client, KnowledgeBase, "embedding", query_vector, k=5, ef_runtime=100
)

It returns a list of (document_id, score) tuples. ef_runtime is passed to the HNSW query: larger values search more of the graph, which raises recall and costs time. If the search itself fails (for example, the index does not exist), the function logs a warning and returns [].

How to use the results in a RAG prompt

Retrieval gives you passages. Build the prompt with any LLM client:

hits = await search(redis_client, question, k=3)
context = "\n\n".join(text for _, text in hits)
prompt = f"Answer using only this context:\n\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"

For a full agent with conversation memory, see the LangGraph tutorial.

How to filter by metadata

Beanis does not combine a vector query and a field filter in one Redis command. Add an indexed field and intersect in Python:

from beanis import Indexed

class KnowledgeBase(Document):
    text: str
    language: Indexed(str)
    embedding: Annotated[List[float], VectorField(dimensions=1024)]

results = await IndexManager.find_by_vector_similarity(
    redis_client, KnowledgeBase, "embedding", query_vector, k=50
)
docs = [await KnowledgeBase.get(doc_id) for doc_id, _ in results]
english = [d for d in docs if d is not None and d.language == "en"][:5]

Ask for a larger k than you need, since some hits will be filtered out. For a large filtered subset, await KnowledgeBase.find(language="en") gives you the matching documents directly.

Choosing an embedding model

The example uses jina-embeddings-v4, as the simple-rag example does. Its vectors are 2048-dimensional by default; truncate_dim=1024 keeps them at 1024. It is built on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, so a GPU helps, and its license is the Qwen Research License, so check it before commercial use. Any other model works: set dimensions to its output size and embed queries and documents with the same model.

Questions people ask

Do I need Redis Stack for vector search? Yes. The vector index is a RediSearch index (FT.CREATE), so you need Redis Stack or another Redis build with RediSearch. Beanis’s other features run on plain Redis.

Can I use OpenAI embeddings instead of Jina? Yes. Set VectorField(dimensions=1536) for text-embedding-3-small, and use the same model for documents and queries.

When is the vector index created? During init_beanis(), not on the first insert. Beanis skips creation if the index already exists.

How do I delete a document from the index? Call await doc.delete_self() or await KnowledgeBase.delete(doc_id). RediSearch drops a hash from its index when the hash is deleted.

Why does search return nothing? Check that the first init_beanis() run printed Created vector index (later runs find the index and print nothing), that dimensions matches your embedding length, and that queries use the same model as the documents.

Links

  • PyPI: pypi.org/project/beanis
  • GitHub: github.com/andreim14/beanis
  • Docs: andreim14.github.io/beanis
  • Example: beanis-examples/simple-rag
  • Redis vector search: redis.io docs
entry.summary: Store text and embeddings in Redis Stack with the Beanis ODM, let it create the HNSW index, and retrieve the top-k passages for a RAG prompt. Complete async Python code.

entry.title: Beanis: an async Redis ODM for Python with Pydantic models

link.title: Beanis: an async Redis ODM for Python with Pydantic models

entry.content:
Beanis is an open-source async object-document mapper (ODM) for Redis. You define Pydantic models, and Beanis stores them as Redis hashes, maintains secondary indexes and turns them back into typed objects. By the end of this post you will have a working model with validation, index queries and TTLs.

   
Package pip install beanis (0.2.0)
Code github.com/andreim14/beanis (Apache 2.0)
Docs andreim14.github.io/beanis
Requirements Python 3.9+, Pydantic (>=1.10,<3), redis-py 5+ async client, Redis 5+. No Redis modules for core features; vector search needs RediSearch (Redis Stack).

Minimal example

Start Redis (docker run -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7), then:

import asyncio
from typing import Optional

from redis.asyncio import Redis
from beanis import Document, Indexed, init_beanis


class Product(Document):
    name: str
    description: Optional[str] = None
    price: Indexed(float)          # sorted set index: range queries
    category: Indexed(str)         # set index: exact match
    stock: int = 0


async def main():
    client = Redis(host="localhost", port=6379, decode_responses=True)
    await init_beanis(database=client, document_models=[Product])

    product = Product(name="Tony's Chocolonely", price=5.95, category="chocolate", stock=100)
    await product.insert()

    found = await Product.get(product.id)
    print(found.name, found.price)

    cheap = await Product.find(price__lte=10.0)
    chocolate = await Product.find(category="chocolate", price__gte=1.0)
    print(len(cheap), len(chocolate))

    await product.update(price=6.95, stock=150)
    print(await product.increment_field("stock", -1))  # atomic HINCRBY

    await product.delete_self()
    await client.close()


asyncio.run(main())

decode_responses=True is required: Beanis expects strings back from Redis, not bytes.

Why Beanis exists

Redis is fast, but the code around a hash is repetitive. Every read converts strings back to numbers, every nested object goes through json.dumps and json.loads, and every secondary index is a sorted set or set you update by hand:

raw = await redis.hgetall(f"Product:{product_id}")
product = {
    "name": raw["name"],
    "price": float(raw["price"]),
    "category": json.loads(raw["category"]),
}

With Beanis that becomes await Product.get(product_id), and you get a validated Product back.

I like Beanie, the MongoDB ODM. Beanis started as a fork of it and keeps its style (Pydantic models, init_* call, event hooks) on top of plain Redis commands. Compared with Redis OM, Beanis does not need the RedisJSON or RediSearch modules for documents, indexes or geo queries.

How Beanis stores a document in Redis

For Product with id abc:

Redis key Type Holds
Product:abc hash the fields; nested models, lists and dicts as JSON strings
all:Product sorted set every id, scored by insert time (used by all() and count())
idx:Product:price sorted set id scored by price (int and float fields)
idx:Product:category:chocolate set ids with that exact value (other indexed types)
idx:Product:location geo set ids by coordinates (GeoPoint fields)

The key prefix defaults to the class name. Set key_prefix in class Settings to change it.

How to query by index

find() takes keyword filters on indexed fields and returns a list. Several filters are combined with AND (set intersection).

await Product.find(category="chocolate")                # exact match on a set index
await Product.find(price__gte=10, price__lte=50)        # range on a sorted set index
await Product.find(category="chocolate", price__lte=5)  # both

Range operators work on int and float fields. Use __gte and __lte. Strings, booleans and dates are indexed for exact match only. Filtering on a field that is not indexed raises ValueError.

Indexes are written by insert(). In 0.2.0, insert_many() and update() write the hash only, so use insert() for documents you want to find by index.

For everything else there are id-based and scan-style helpers:

products = await Product.get_many([id1, id2, id3])   # pipelined, returns None for missing ids
page = await Product.all(skip=0, limit=20, sort_desc=True)
total = await Product.count()
exists = await Product.exists(id1)

How to validate data before it reaches Redis

Models are Pydantic models, so constraints are checked when you build the object:

from pydantic import Field, ValidationError
from beanis import Document, Indexed


class User(Document):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    age: int = Field(ge=13, le=120)
    score: Indexed(int) = 0


try:
    User(username="ab", age=200)
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e)  # two errors, nothing written to Redis

Reads skip validation by default (model_construct), because the data came from your own writes. Set use_validation_on_fetch = True in Settings if you want reads validated too.

How to expire documents with TTL

await product.insert(ttl=3600)     # expires in one hour
await product.set_ttl(7200)
print(await product.get_ttl())
await product.persist()            # remove the expiry

You can also set default_ttl in Settings.

How to run code before or after insert, update, delete

from beanis import Document, before_event, after_event, Insert, Update


class Order(Document):
    total: float
    status: str = "pending"

    @before_event(Insert)
    async def check_total(self):
        if self.total < 0:
            raise ValueError("total cannot be negative")

    @after_event(Update)
    async def log_update(self):
        print(f"order {self.id} updated")

How to store custom types (NumPy, your own classes)

NumPy arrays and PyTorch tensors are registered automatically when those libraries are installed. For your own types, register an encoder and decoder that convert to and from a string:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from beanis import register_type


@dataclass
class Money:
    amount: str
    currency: str


register_type(
    Money,
    encoder=lambda m: f"{m.amount}:{m.currency}",
    decoder=lambda s: Money(*s.split(":")),
)

register_encoder(type_) and register_decoder(type_) do the same as decorators.

Geo and vector fields

Two index types go beyond sets and sorted sets:

  • GeoPoint with an index uses GEOADD and GEORADIUS. See the restaurant finder tutorial.
  • VectorField(dimensions=...) creates a RediSearch HNSW index at init_beanis time. This one needs Redis Stack. See the RAG tutorial.

Performance

The README reports about 8% overhead over plain redis-py for get-by-id. The benchmark script behind that number is not in the repo, so treat it as indicative. The design choices that keep reads cheap are visible in the source: msgspec for JSON parsing, model_construct() instead of full validation on reads, and pipelines for insert_many, get_many and delete_many.

When not to use Beanis

  • Plain key-value caching, where a GET/SET is all you need.
  • You need full-text search or JSON path queries: use RediSearch and RedisJSON directly, or Redis OM.
  • You need relations or aggregations. Beanis has neither (Beanie’s Link, aggregation pipelines and migrations were removed).

Questions people ask

What is the difference between Beanis and Redis OM? Redis OM relies on the RediSearch module for queries (and RedisJSON for JSON models). Beanis stores hashes and builds its indexes from plain sets, sorted sets and geo sets, so it runs on stock Redis.

Does Beanis work with Pydantic v2? Yes. The package declares pydantic>=1.10,<3, and the geo type uses Pydantic v2 validators.

Can I use Indexed[float] like in Beanie? No. In Beanis Indexed is a function: write Indexed(float), or Annotated[float, IndexedField()].

Is update() atomic? update(**fields) writes the given fields with one HSET. For counters use increment_field(), which is a single HINCRBY (or HINCRBYFLOAT for floats).

Which Python versions are supported? Python 3.9 and later, per the package metadata on PyPI.
